news.h: TMK Chemical to buy CCM from Batu Kawan for RM939.9m
news.body: TMK Chemical Bhd has agreed to acquire Chemical Company of Malaysia Bhd (CCM) from Batu Kawan Bhd and its wholly-owned unit Enternal Edge Sdn Bhd for RM939.9m. TMK said the purchase will be satisfied through RM438.5m cash and the issuance of 262.5m new TMK shares to Batu Kawan at RM1.9098 apiece. The new shares will see Batu Kawan acquire a 20.8% stake in TMK's enlarged share capital. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: The consideration reconciles exactly and the arithmetic is worth doing, because the item prints the parts but not the check. 262.5m new shares at RM1.9098 is RM501.3m of paper; added to RM438.5m of cash that is RM939.8m, against the RM939.9m headline - agreement to within rounding, computed here. So the deal is 46.7% cash and 53.3% equity, a split the item never states.

The share issuance implies a share count the item does not give. If 262.5m new shares represent 20.8% of the enlarged capital, the enlarged base is about 1,262m shares and TMK's pre-deal base about 999.5m - both derived here. Batu Kawan therefore moves from no disclosed stake to being a one-fifth owner of the buyer, which means it is not exiting the chemicals business so much as swapping a subsidiary for a fifth of a larger listed one.

Batu Kawan is on both sides of two different transactions on this board within three sessions. On 18 September this board carried Batu Kawan raising its MKH Oil Palm stake to 79.6% after a mandatory general offer at 66.26 sen - a deal in which the independent adviser recommended REJECT, and in which Kenanga Investment Bank acted as independent adviser to the parent, MKH Bhd. Today Batu Kawan is the seller of CCM. The digest connects the two nowhere; the link is drawn here, and the common thread is portfolio reshaping rather than any stated strategy, because neither item gives one.

Nothing here can be valued, because no financials for CCM appear. No revenue, no earnings, no net assets, no historical purchase price, no earnings multiple and no completion date is given, so RM939.9m cannot be tested against anything. The item also names no independent adviser for this transaction, no approval conditions and no shareholder-vote requirement.

This board holds no Kenanga research coverage of TMK Chemical, CCM or Batu Kawan, and the 21 September bundle - two sector updates, two company updates and four Economic Viewpoints - contains no chemicals report. The nearest Kenanga figures on this board for the chemical complex come from PCHEM, carried on 17 September at MARKET PERFORM with an RM4.24 target; this edition's own top-loser table shows PCHEM at RM4.71, down 3.1% on the 18 September session.

news.h: Vestland bags third contract this month, this time for RM107.6m on slope mitigation
news.body: Vestland Bhd has secured a job worth RM107.6m to undertake slope mitigation and related works at a reservoir catchment area in Terengganu. The contract awarded to its wholly owned subsidiary Vestland Infra Sdn Bhd will begin in October and be completed by May 2029, the construction and civil engineering firm said in a bourse filing. "This contract further strengthens Vestland's presence in the infrastructure sector and reflects our continued progress in expanding our civil engineering portfolio," their joint managing director said in a statement. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: The run-rate is the only number the item permits and it is modest. October 2026 to May 2029 is about 31 months, so RM107.6m works out at roughly RM3.5m a month, or RM41.6m a year - arithmetic here. No margin, no retention terms and no performance bond is stated, so the earnings contribution cannot be sized at all.

The most material figure is not in the digest item. The Edge Malaysia's 18 September stocks-to-watch report on the same award states that Vestland has won RM1.6b of new contracts year-to-date and carries a total outstanding order book of RM2.0b. On that base this RM107.6m award is 6.7% of the year's wins and 5.4% of the order book, both computed here - which reframes a headline that reads as a third win in a month into a routine addition to a book that is already twenty times its size.

Ownership and counterparty are unequal in disclosure. Vestland Infra Sdn Bhd is described as wholly owned, so the full amount accrues to the group with no minority leakage - the same clean structure recorded for Enproserve on 18 September. But the awarding party is not named anywhere, only the asset type: a reservoir catchment area in Terengganu. Whether the client is a state body, a federal agency or a private owner is not established from the retrieved source.

The quoted line is corporate positioning rather than information. The joint managing director's statement - that the contract 'further strengthens Vestland's presence in the infrastructure sector and reflects our continued progress in expanding our civil engineering portfolio' - contains no figure, no target and no comparison, and the item does not name the executive.

Construction awards remain the densest recurring theme on this board and this edition adds three at once. Recent entries: Citaglobal's RM82.1m residential college subcontract (14 September), GFM's RM37.4m Pengerang turnaround works (15 September), Exsim Hospitality's RM42.5m building works (15 September), Crest Builder's RM56.9m M&E subcontract and PTT Synergy's RM83.3m Klang earthworks (17 September), Enproserve's RM12.3m Putrajaya maintenance contract (18 September), and today Vestland's RM107.6m, TSR Capital's RM158.0m and Jati Tinggi's RM72.8m. Vestland's is the second-largest of the nine and the longest-dated. This board holds no Kenanga coverage of Vestland and the 21 September bundle carries no construction report.

news.h: Jati Tinggi bags RM72.8m data centre-linked job in Selangor; its third contract win in a month
news.body: Engineering and infrastructure specialist Jati Tinggi Group Bhd has won a RM72.8m contract to design and build a high-voltage 275kV cable connection to a data centre's landing station in Banting Technology Park, Selangor. This marks Jati Tinggi's third contract win in the last 30 days. The group said its wholly-owned Jati Tinggi Holding Sdn Bhd accepted the Letter of Award for the project from an undisclosed customer on Sept 18. The contract, in effect upon acceptance, is scheduled to conclude on Jan 15, 2027. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: The timetable is the striking part and it is far more aggressive than anything else on this board. The Letter of Award was accepted on 18 September and the contract concludes on 15 January 2027 - about four months - so RM72.8m implies a burn of roughly RM18.2m a month, computed here. By comparison, TSR Capital's RM158.0m in this same edition runs about RM4.4m a month over three years and Vestland's RM107.6m about RM3.5m a month over 31 months. Either the recognition is heavily front-loaded or the scope is already substantially engineered; the item does not say which.

The order book context comes from outside the digest. The Edge Malaysia's parallel 21 September report on the same award states that the win lifts Jati Tinggi's order book to about RM1.1b. On that base a RM72.8m award is 6.6% of the book, computed here - so the significance of this item is the third-win-in-30-days cadence rather than its size.

This is the clearest read-across in the edition to Kenanga's own bundle, and the digest draws none of it. The contract is a 275kV high-voltage cable connection to a data centre landing station - grid connection work, not IT. Kenanga's TENAGA Company Update in the same bundle states that data centre investment of more than 8,000MW is expected by 2035 with about 700MW coming on stream this year, and its Renewable Energy Sector Update puts Malaysia's secured data centre maximum demand at about 8.35GW today against a PETRA projection of about 21GW by 2040, arguing that faster renewable adoption 'should support longer-term grid connectivity and reinforcement needs'. This award is that thesis arriving as a contract.

The counterparty is undisclosed and that matters for a data centre job. No customer name, no operator, no capacity for the data centre being connected and no indication of whether TENAGA is the contracting party appears. Jati Tinggi Holding Sdn Bhd is stated to be wholly owned, so the full value accrues to the group.

Banting Technology Park places this in the Selangor cluster rather than Johor, which is where most of this board's data centre activity has sat. Related entries: KGB's RM1.83b semiconductor wafer-fab award (15 September), NuEnergy's RM48.8m rooftop solar investment (15 September) and Reservoir Link's 200MWac Sarawak solar PPA (18 September). This board holds no Kenanga rating on Jati Tinggi, and no report in the 21 September bundle covers engineering or cable contractors.

news.h: ES Sunlogy bags electrical services subcontract for Johor serviced apartments
news.body: ES Sunlogy Bhd said it has secured a RM15.6m subcontract for electrical phase two services works for a serviced apartment development in Johor. ES Sunlogy said its wholly-owned subsidiary Savelite Engineering Sdn Bhd was awarded the subcontract by JY Consult PLT, acting on behalf of Parkland Southern Sdn Bhd. The project involves the development of a 36-storey serviced apartment comprising two towers with a total of 1,078 units, a seven-storey podium and a guardhouse. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is the smallest of the edition's five corporate items by an order of magnitude - RM15.6m against RM939.9m, RM158.0m, RM107.6m and RM72.8m - and the only one where the item gives enough detail to price the work per unit. Across 1,078 apartments, RM15.6m is about RM14,500 of electrical works per unit, computed here. No duration, no start date, no completion date and no margin is stated anywhere, so nothing can be annualised.

The contracting chain has three parties and only one of them is the developer. Savelite Engineering Sdn Bhd, described as wholly owned by ES Sunlogy, was awarded the subcontract by JY Consult PLT, which is acting on behalf of Parkland Southern Sdn Bhd. That makes ES Sunlogy a second-tier subcontractor on the project - further from the developer than the M&E and earthworks awards this board carried on 17 September - and the item names no main contractor at all.

It is explicitly phase two, which is the detail that limits what can be read into it. The scope is 'electrical phase two services works', so a phase one exists and is not described: no value, no completion status, no indication of whether ES Sunlogy held it. Whether this is a repeat award to an incumbent or a new entry cannot be established from the retrieved source.

The building is specified more precisely than the contract. A 36-storey development, two towers, 1,078 units, a seven-storey podium and a guardhouse - but no gross development value, no location within Johor and no developer profile. So the only way to gauge the counterparty's standing is the project's own scale, which is substantial for a single subcontract of this size.

Johor residential supply is the context the item omits, and this board has carried the other side of it. On 11 September the government flagged that unsold affordable and mid-priced homes make up an increasing share of Malaysia's growing property overhang; on 18 September Glomac's return to profit came entirely from progress on existing schemes rather than new sales. A 1,078-unit serviced apartment scheme adds to that supply. This board holds no Kenanga coverage of ES Sunlogy, and the property names in Kenanga's peer table in today's ECOWLD report - IOIPG, LBS, MAHSING, MRCB, PARAMOUNT, SPSETIA, SIMEPROP, SUNWAY, UOADEV - do not include the developer here.

news.h: TSR Capital bags RM158.0m PKNS contract for Selangor building works
news.body: TSR Capital Bhd said it has secured a contract worth about RM158.0m for building works in Selangor. TSR Capital said its wholly owned subsidiary TSR Bina Sdn Bhd had accepted a letter of award from Perbadanan Kemajuan Negeri Selangor (PKNS) for the construction and completion of the building works. TSR Capital said the contract has a duration of about three years and is scheduled for completion by the first quarter of 2029. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is the largest contract award in the edition and the second-largest this board has carried in a month, behind KGB's RM1.83b semiconductor wafer-fab job on 15 September. Over a stated three-year duration, RM158.0m is about RM4.4m a month or RM52.7m a year - arithmetic here, and the only run-rate the item permits, since no margin, no payment milestones and no escalation clause is given.

The counterparty is a state development corporation, which puts this in the same public-sector bucket as the 18 September Enproserve award from Perbadanan Putrajaya, and it is the second time in four sessions that a statutory body rather than a private client has been the payer. PKNS is Selangor's state economic development corporation; the item gives no project name, no site and no building type beyond 'building works', so what is being built cannot be established from the retrieved source.

Ownership is clean and stated: TSR Bina Sdn Bhd is described as wholly owned, so the whole RM158.0m accrues to the group at the revenue line. The item gives no existing order book, no year-to-date wins and no revenue base, which is the gap that The Edge Malaysia's parallel reporting filled for Vestland and Jati Tinggi in this same edition but not for TSR Capital - so the award's materiality to the company cannot be judged here.

The completion date sits one quarter beyond Vestland's. Scheduled completion is the first quarter of 2029 against Vestland's May 2029, and both are longer-dated than anything else in the edition. Nothing in the item is due to complete inside the current or next financial year, and no revenue-recognition profile is described.

Selangor is the edition's centre of gravity and no source draws the line. Two of the five corporate items are Selangor projects - this one and Jati Tinggi's 275kV data centre connection in Banting Technology Park - and this board carried Selangor projecting more than RM100.0b of investment value for 2026 on 9 September. This board holds no Kenanga coverage of TSR Capital, and the 21 September bundle contains no construction or building-materials report.

macro.h: Trump-Xi showdown casts shadow over global economy
macro.body: US President Donald Trump's talks with China's Xi Jinping is set to be the week's pivotal event, covering crucial issues from tariffs to technology related to the world's two largest economies. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is the thinnest item in the edition and the one Kenanga's own research puts at the centre of the week. The digest gives no date, no venue, no format, no agenda and no negotiating position - only that talks are 'set to be the week's pivotal event' covering 'tariffs to technology'. Yet Kenanga's Bond Market Weekly Outlook in this same bundle names the Trump-Xi meeting twice as a key driver, for both Malaysian government securities and US Treasuries, and states that 'any trade or de-escalation breakthrough would likely reduce UST duration demand'.

That gives the item a directional read the digest does not supply. On Kenanga's framing, a breakthrough is a risk-positive, duration-negative event: it would push US Treasury yields up, not down. The same note says UST yields should 'trade within a narrow range in the week ahead' pending this and US labour data, and that market sentiment 'will remain highly sensitive to geopolitical and trade developments'. This connection is drawn here; neither source states it in one place.

Nothing about the meeting is confirmed in the retrieved source. No meeting date, no location, no attendee list beyond the two principals, no prior round referenced and no stated deliverable. It cannot be treated as a scheduled event so much as an expectation, and a later edition has nothing measurable to compare it against.

Both halves of the pairing already sit on this board separately and this is the first item to put them together. The United States has run an unbroken sequence of upside data surprises since late August into a Fed that hiked 25bps on 16 September; China appears in this very edition holding its loan prime rates unchanged for a sixteenth month with subdued domestic demand. The item frames them as the world's two largest economies without giving a single figure for either.

No report in the 21 September bundle carries a Kenanga view on US-China trade policy, and no listed company or sector is named. The nearest exposure on this board is the electrical and electronics export channel - Kenanga's own External Trade Economic Viewpoint in this bundle puts August E&E exports at +66.5% YoY and shipments to the United States at a record +139.1% - which is the concentration that a tariff outcome would act on, and which the item does not mention.

macro.h: Inflation edges up to 1.9% as energy costs seep back into prices
macro.body: Headline inflation increased to 1.9% YoY in August (Jul: 1.8%), slightly above our forecast and consensus of 1.8%. We lower our 2026 inflation forecast to 1.9% (from 2.1%), as subsidies continue to absorb the global energy shock. (See Economic Viewpoint: Malaysia Consumer Price Index)
takeaways: The headline missed upward while the forecast was cut, which is the tension in the item. August headline inflation came in at 1.9% against Kenanga's own and consensus estimates of 1.8%, yet the same note lowers the full-year 2026 forecast to 1.9% from 2.1%. The reconciliation is in the base: at 1.9% year-to-date-consistent running and four months to go, a 2.1% full-year outcome would require a sharp fourth-quarter acceleration that the note explicitly does not expect, partly because of the electricity measure. That arithmetic is drawn here; the item states only the two numbers.

Core went the other way and the note says why. Core inflation eased to 1.7% YoY from 1.8%, which Kenanga attributes 'only to a high base' - on a monthly basis core rose 0.3%, the same as the headline, after two flat months. So the month was a broad monthly pickup, with 10 of 13 groups posting gains, dressed as a core deceleration by the year-ago comparison.

The energy transmission channel is named precisely and it is not the pump. Kenanga states that global energy prices are reaching consumers 'through unsubsidised channels rather than at the pump': RON95 stays fixed at RM1.99 under BUDI95, while domestic airfares rose 15.0% MoM and the fuel surcharge for Peninsular households using more than 600kWh rose to 3.80 sen/kWh in August from 3.59 sen in July. This is the same surcharge that TENAGA is now absorbing - see the TENAGA row in this bundle - so the August CPI print captures the cost that the 800kWh measure is designed to stop passing through from September.

The policy conclusion is a hold and the note gives two independent reasons for it. Kenanga expects BNM to keep the OPR at 2.75% through 2026 'even as the Fed and ECB resume hiking', because with inflation below 2.0% the real policy rate stays positive; and it reads the September MGS curve steepening as coming from the long end - 'rising global term premium rather than bets on domestic tightening'. The second point is the same argument this board carried from the 17 September Economic Viewpoint, now restated with a week more curve data behind it.

The comparison the item invites is with the rest of the world, and Malaysia is an outlier at the bottom. Kenanga's own global table in the note prints August inflation at 3.4% for the US, 3.2% for the EU, 3.1% for the UK and South Korea, 3.2% for Indonesia, 2.5% for Thailand, 1.9% for Japan and 0.8% for China. Malaysia's 1.9% sits level with Japan and above only China, which is the practical content of 'subsidies continue to absorb the global energy shock'.

macro.h: Malaysia's August exports surge 45.5% to RM191.05b
macro.body: Malaysia's exports rose 45.5% year-on-year (y-o-y) to RM191.05b in August 2026, driven by stronger shipments of manufactured and mining goods. According to a statement by the Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry (MITI), total trade increased 43.4% y-o-y to RM354.01b, while imports grew 41.1% to RM162.96b. (The Malaysian Reserve)
takeaways: The three figures are internally consistent and give a trade balance the item does not print. Exports of RM191.05b less imports of RM162.96b is a surplus of RM28.09b, and the two summed give RM354.01b of total trade - both computed here, and the surplus matches the RM28.1b in Kenanga's own External Trade Economic Viewpoint in this bundle exactly. That note adds that the surplus beat both consensus (RM25.3b) and Kenanga's own estimate (RM25.9b), and widened from RM22.5b in July.

At +45.5% the growth rate also implies the year-ago base: RM191.05b divided by 1.455 gives about RM131.3b for August 2025, arithmetic here and printed nowhere. The scale of the surge is easier to read that way - close to RM60b of additional monthly exports year-on-year.

An independent, named, same-day source confirms the year-to-date claim Kenanga builds its forecast on. MATRADE, reported by the New Straits Times on 21 September, puts January-August 2026 exports at RM1.356 trillion, up 31.2% from RM1.033 trillion - the identical 31.2% year-to-date figure Kenanga's note carries. RM1.356 trillion over eight months annualises to about RM2.03 trillion at a flat run-rate, computed here, which is the arithmetic behind Kenanga's statement that exports are 'on track to exceed RM2.0 trillion mark this year'.

The concentration risk is the part neither the item nor MITI addresses. Kenanga's note shows electrical and electronic exports at +66.5% YoY and 48.4% of total exports, with shipments to the United States at a record +139.1%. So roughly half the export book is one product category, and its fastest-growing destination is the counterparty in this edition's lead global item on Trump-Xi trade talks. MATRADE's own colour runs the other way - exports to 40 countries have already surpassed their full-year 2025 values, with emerging markets led by Namibia (+430.6%), Angola (+215.4%), Ethiopia (+51.2%), Tanzania (+50.2%) and Bangladesh (+20.2%) - but those are small bases against a US channel of this size.

Kenanga raised its 2026 export forecast to 28.5% from 19.0% on the back of this print and maintained its 2026 GDP growth forecast at 5.3% (2025: 5.2%), the same standing figure this board has carried since 1 September. It also flags the sequential picture that the headline hides: exports fell 1.3% MoM and imports 4.7% MoM in August, which the note calls a typical seasonal correction after July's rebound, and it expects export growth to slow in 2H26 as favourable base effects fade.

macro.h: BNM flags rising costs, liquidity pressure on SMEs
macro.body: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are facing greater liquidity pressure as global supply disruptions push up operating costs and working-capital requirements, according to Bank Negara Malaysia's (BNM) assessment presented to the government. (The Malaysian Reserve)
takeaways: It is the only domestic downside signal in an edition otherwise full of upside, and it carries no numbers at all. No count of affected SMEs, no credit or default figure, no sector breakdown, no financing facility, no date for the assessment and no government response appears. The mechanism is stated in one clause - global supply disruptions raising operating costs and working-capital requirements - and nothing is quantified against it.

Set beside the rest of the edition the contrast is stark. The same digest carries exports up 45.5%, a trade surplus of RM28.1b, inflation contained at 1.9% and a Kenanga export forecast raised to 28.5%. Aggregate external demand and small-business liquidity are pointing in opposite directions, and nothing in the digest reconciles them - the grouping is made here.

The channel BNM describes is the one Kenanga's own CPI note identifies as live. That note states that global energy prices are reaching the economy 'through unsubsidised channels rather than at the pump', naming airfares and freight-sensitive food items - which is a cost-of-goods effect that lands on firms before it lands on consumer prices. Working capital rising because input costs rise is the same transmission seen from the corporate side. Neither source draws the link.

It has a policy edge the item does not state. Kenanga expects BNM to hold the OPR at 2.75% through 2026, and an SME liquidity squeeze is precisely the condition that argues against tightening into a supply shock - the same argument Kenanga made against the Fed's September hike, recorded on this board on 17 September. That BNM is presenting this assessment to the government rather than acting on it through rates points to a fiscal or credit-guarantee response instead, and the item names neither.

Budget 2027 is the obvious destination and the item makes no mention of it. This board has tracked the budget since 24 August (cost-of-living focus), 26 August (Home Ownership Campaign and EV infrastructure proposals) and 15 September (the Ministry of Finance's consultation tour for industry, NGO and public input). No report in the 21 September bundle covers SMEs, banking or credit conditions, and this board holds no Kenanga figures on SME lending.

macro.h: 1.25% done, two dissents push the next hike to 1Q27
macro.body: Split vote: The Bank of Japan (BoJ) raised the overnight call rate (OCR) by 25 bps to 1.25% in a 7-2 vote, just three months after June's hike. BoJ keeps normalising, but a divided board pushes our next hike call to 1Q27. (See Economic Viewpoint: BoJ Monetary Policy Decision (17-18 September))
takeaways: Kenanga called this one right and says so only implicitly. Its own meeting-schedule table shows the house outlook for the 17-18 September meeting as '25 bps hike' against a BoJ decision of '25 bps hike' - the only match in the table. For the 15-16 June meeting the same table shows a house call of 'No change' against an actual 25bps hike. So the record on the two 2026 hikes is one hit, one miss, and the note does not draw attention to the miss.

The dissenters are named, which is unusual for this board's central-bank items. Toichiro Asada argued the economy was not strong enough to justify a hike with core CPI running below 2.0%; Ayano Sato judged that economic and price developments had not accelerated materially. Both dissents are on the dovish side, which is what makes the 7-2 split an argument for a slower pace rather than a faster one - and it is why Kenanga pushes its next hike call to 1Q27 rather than expecting a quarterly cadence.

Three different Japanese inflation figures appear across this one bundle without being reconciled. This note says core CPI 'has risen moderately to a 1.5-2.0% range' and that August core eased; the BoJ's own July forecast table in the same note has fiscal 2026 core CPI at a +2.3% to +2.7% range with a +2.5% median; and Kenanga's CPI Economic Viewpoint in the same bundle prints Japan's headline inflation flat at 1.9% for both July and August. The three measure different things - underlying, BoJ core ex-fresh-food and headline - and no source says so. Reported as printed rather than resolved; see the flag on the BoJ row.

The currency call is the part with a live P&L attached. Kenanga maintains its end-2026 USDJPY forecast at 154.0 while conceding that near-term pricing of a second Fed hike plus elevated oil could push the pair to 158-160. This edition's own forex table prints USD/YEN at 156.88 on the 18 September session, up 0.79% - already 1.9% above the year-end forecast and inside the lower half of the stated near-term range, computed here. The note names the trigger explicitly: the Fed holding rather than delivering a second hike; without it, '154.0 is at risk to the upside'.

At 1.25% Japan remains the second-lowest policy rate in Kenanga's own table of thirteen, above only Thailand at 1.00%, and the note states that the rate 'sits inside the lower end of the BoJ's estimated neutral range for the first time' without printing that range. Malaysia appears in the same table at 2.75% with its last move a 25bps cut in July 2025 - fourteen months of no change against a BoJ that has now moved twice in three months.

macro.h: China keeps benchmark lending rates unchanged for 16th month in September
macro.body: China kept its benchmark lending rates unchanged for the 16th straight month on Sunday, in line with market expectations. The steady loan prime rates underscored the limited scope for fresh monetary easing after some major global central banks recently adopted a more hawkish stance, even as the yuan continued to strengthen. (Reuters)
takeaways: The 16-month count can be checked against Kenanga's own table in the same bundle, and it holds. The BoJ Economic Viewpoint's policy-rate table shows China's 1-year Loan Prime Rate at 3.00% with its last change a 10bps cut in May 2025. June 2025 through September 2026 inclusive is sixteen monthly fixings with no change - arithmetic here, and neither source states the cross-check.

China is the only major bond market in Kenanga's weekly table where yields have fallen this year. Its Bond Market Weekly Outlook prints the 10-year Chinese government bond at 1.685%, down 17.0bps year-to-date and down 9.7bps year-on-year, against 10-year yields up 42.5bps in Malaysia, 82.9bps in the US, 66.3bps in the euro area, 81.6bps in the UK and 92.3bps in Japan. That is the market expression of the 'limited scope for fresh monetary easing' the item describes - China is already the easiest curve in the set.

Kenanga's diagnosis of the domestic economy is more negative than the item's. Its CPI Economic Viewpoint in this bundle records Chinese inflation at 0.8% in August (Jul: 0.5%), says the pickup came from higher energy costs tied to the West Asia war lifting transport prices, and states that 'domestic demand stays subdued, and export resilience continues to mask weak consumption' - adding that expanded loan-interest subsidies and signalled fiscal support are 'piecemeal measures' that 'have yet to spark a broader recovery'. The item calls the hold expected; Kenanga calls the policy mix insufficient.

The yuan clause is the constraint the item names but does not size. Holding rates 'even as the yuan continued to strengthen' is the opposite of the usual framing - a strengthening currency normally creates room to ease, not less of it. No exchange rate, no move and no time frame is given, and the digest's own forex table carries no CNY pair, so the strength claim cannot be verified from the retrieved sources.

Timing is worth noting: the fixing was on a Sunday, 20 September, which is why a decision reaches a Monday digest. No report in the 21 September bundle carries a Kenanga view on China, and China's only other appearance in this edition is as the counterparty in the lead global item on Trump-Xi trade talks.

macro.h: US factory output unexpectedly falls for first time this year
macro.body: US factory output unexpectedly declined for the first time this year as production of business equipment cooled and manufacturers grappled with higher input costs. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: This breaks a run this board had explicitly flagged as unbroken. On 18 September this row recorded that 'not one US activity print in that sequence has disappointed', listing service-sector-led acceleration (24 August), strong services demand (4 September), surging non-farm payrolls with unemployment steady at 4.1% (7 September), producer prices as expected (11 September), consumer inflation picking up (14 September), retail sales rebounding more than expected (17 September) and jobless claims falling against expectations (18 September). Today is the first downside surprise in that sequence, and it is the first fall in factory output this year.

Nothing in it is quantified. No index level, no percentage change, no consensus estimate, no prior month and no capacity-utilisation figure is printed, so the size of the decline cannot be established from the retrieved source. Two causes are named without being sized either: production of business equipment cooling, and manufacturers grappling with higher input costs.

The second cause is the one that connects to the rest of the edition. Higher input costs for US manufacturers is the same energy shock that this edition's EU windfall-tax item, Kenanga's CPI note and the Malaysian electricity measure are all responses to - with Nymex crude at USD100.3 a barrel on the 18 September session. A supply-side squeeze on output is a different problem from weak demand, and a funds rate does not fix it; that is precisely the argument Kenanga used to call the Fed's 16 September hike a policy error, recorded on this board on 17 September.

Kenanga's own bond note in this same bundle, published the same morning, reads the US data the other way and does not mention factory output. It cites 'strong August retail sales and a surprise decline in initial jobless claims' as suggesting the Fed may hold rates steady for an extended period, and states a base case that 'the latest Fed hike marks the end of the tightening cycle' with policy rates unchanged through end-2027. This print is the first data point in weeks that would argue for that hold from the weak side rather than the strong side, and neither source connects the two.

Market context from this edition's own tables, with no causal link to be read into it: the Dow fell 0.18% to 51,682.6 on the 18 September session while the S&P 500 rose 0.17% to 7,650.5 and the NASDAQ 0.39% to 26,522.5 - a split that leaves the industrial index alone in the red. Kenanga's bond table shows the 10-year US Treasury at 4.996%, up 2.9bps on the week and 82.9bps year-to-date.

macro.h: EU ministers to discuss taxing windfall profits of energy companies as oil prices surge
macro.body: European Union finance ministers will discuss on Friday whether to impose an EU-wide windfall tax on energy companies benefiting from a surge in oil and gas prices following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, with further talks expected in October. (The Edge Malaysia)
takeaways: It is the mirror image of the Malaysian item this board carried three sessions ago, and no source sets them side by side. Malaysia's response to the same energy shock was to widen a consumer subsidy and have the listed utility absorb the cost - RM120m to RM150m borne by TENAGA, covered in this bundle's own Company Update. Europe's proposed response is to tax the energy producers who are gaining from it. Two states, one shock, opposite ends of the value chain; the comparison is drawn here.

Nothing has been decided and nothing is quantified. Finance ministers 'will discuss on Friday whether to impose' a tax, with further talks expected in October - no rate, no threshold, no definition of windfall, no revenue estimate, no company named and no legal instrument. An EU-wide tax would also need unanimity or a qualified majority depending on its legal base, and the item names neither.

The stated trigger is already easing at the margin. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is named as the cause of the price surge, but Kenanga's Bond Market Weekly Outlook in this same bundle records that Brent eased over the week as Saudi Arabia restored part of its East-West pipeline capacity, and this edition's own commodity table shows Nymex crude down 1.58% to USD100.3 a barrel on the 18 September session. Ministers convene into a market that has stopped rising, not one still rising.

It is the first EU fiscal response to the energy shock this board has carried; everything before it was monetary. Prior European entries: the ECB raising rates on 11 September, Lagarde calling the inflation shock longer-lasting (14 September), Kazaks seeing a growing case for more tightening (15 September), and Bailey declining to validate market pricing of four BOE hikes (18 September). Kenanga's own CPI note puts euro-area inflation at 3.2% in August with energy inflation at 14.3% - which is the number that makes a windfall tax politically available.

No report in the 21 September bundle carries a Kenanga view on European energy policy, and no listed Malaysian company is affected by the measure directly. The indirect channel this board does hold is crude: Kenanga's oil and gas coverage on this board runs through KEYFIELD (18 September), DAYANG, VELESTO, UZMA, ARMADA, WASCO and MISC, all of which benefit from higher upstream activity rather than from refined-product margins - so an EU tax on producers has no clean read-across to any of them.

macro.h: Euro zone current account surplus narrows in July
macro.body: The euro zone's current account surplus narrowed in July to EUR27.6b from EUR35.1b a month earlier, European Central Bank data showed on Friday. (Reuters)
takeaways: The one computation the item permits: the surplus fell by EUR7.5b, or 21.4%, month on month - arithmetic here, and the percentage is printed nowhere. No year-ago comparative, no share of GDP, no goods-versus-services split and no primary or secondary income breakdown appears, so neither the cause nor the significance can be established from the retrieved source.

The dating is the quiet limitation. This is July data released on Friday 18 September - a lag of about seven weeks - so it predates the September repricing that dominates the rest of the edition: the Fed's 16 September hike, the BoJ's 17-18 September hike, the ECB's own September move and the renewed crude spike. Nothing in this print reflects any of them.

A narrowing external surplus is what an energy-importing bloc looks like when import costs rise, and the item does not make that argument. Kenanga's CPI Economic Viewpoint in this same bundle puts EU inflation at 3.2% in August with energy inflation at 14.3%, attributing it to the Iran war and Hormuz disruption lifting crude, refined products and natural gas costs. A higher energy import bill compresses the goods balance directly. The link is drawn here and is inference, not a stated cause - the item names no component at all.

The market read on the euro was nil on the day. This edition's forex table shows EUR/USD at 1.1486 against 1.1478, up 0.07% on the 18 September session - the smallest move of the six pairs printed, against USD/MYR down 0.42%, USD/YEN up 0.79% and GBP/USD down 0.07%. Kenanga's bond table shows the 10-year euro-area yield at 3.517%, up 1.4bps on the week and 66.3bps year-to-date.

Europe fills two of the edition's nine macro slots for the second time in recent sessions, and this is the second-order one. The other is the proposed EU windfall tax on energy companies, which is about the same shock arriving as fiscal policy; this item is the same shock arriving as an external balance, two months late. No report in the 21 September bundle carries a Kenanga view on the euro area or the ECB beyond the CPI note's observation that, with core inflation easing to 2.4%, it sees 'little appetite to risk a recession over what remains a textbook supply shock'.

reports.name: Automotive Sector Update: Shorter Working Month (Aug-26 TIV)
reports.catalyst: NEUTRAL maintained on the sector after August TIV of 71,428 units fell 3% MoM and 4% YoY on a shorter working month with two public holidays. YTD TIV of 530,478 units (+2%) is described as well within expectation, and the CY26 forecast of 800k units (-3% YoY) is held, matching the Malaysian Automotive Association's own forecast. Two sector top picks are named in Kenanga's own words: BAUTO (OP; TP RM1.30) and SIME (OP; TP RM3.00), both targets unchanged against this board's earlier rows. The month's standout is electric vehicles - a record 8,833 BEV registrations of which the Proton e.MAS 5 alone took 4,770, or 54% - which Kenanga reads as a one-car story, since the rest of the EV market shrank 10% MoM on CBU inventory depletion ahead of CKD localisation.
reports.quote: The record EV month was really a one-car story which we believe was due to other EV brands depleting their CBU inventory, especially BYD (-46% MoM, -35% YoY).
summary: The call and the two picks, with every figure cross-checked against this board's own record. The sector stays NEUTRAL. BAUTO is named a sector top pick at OUTPERFORM with an RM1.30 target - identical to the RM1.30 read from BAUTO's own Results Note PDF on 11 September - and SIME at OUTPERFORM with RM3.00, identical to the RM3.00 read from SIME's own Results Note on 28 August. Two further peer-table entries also agree exactly: MBMR at MARKET PERFORM with RM5.00 (verified 2 September) and TAN CHONG MOTOR at UNDERPERFORM with RM0.390 (27 August). HIL INDUSTRIES at OUTPERFORM with RM0.850 matches the 24 August row. Nothing in this note moves a rating or a target; the peer table's implied upsides are 42.1% for BAUTO and 23.5% for SIME. The stated grounds are specific rather than thematic - BAUTO for a 3.5k-unit order backlog against 1.5k a year ago, premium mid-market Mazda margins and an 11% yield; SIME for 60% Malaysian auto market share, EV leadership in Singapore, Thailand and the Philippines, and an industrials segment running a 7% margin against 1% for its auto segment.

The record EV month, and why Kenanga refuses to read it as one. August produced 8,833 battery-electric registrations, the biggest month on record, of which the Proton e.MAS 5 alone accounted for 4,770 - 54.0% of the total, which reconciles exactly. Strip it out and the remaining EV market fell to 4,063 registrations from 4,535 in July, a 10.4% decline computed here. Kenanga attributes that to other brands depleting completely-built-up inventory while waiting for local assembly, with BYD down 46% MoM and 35% YoY. The structural figures are larger than the monthly ones: BEV registrations have gone 270 units in CY21, 2,600 in CY22, 10,000 in CY23, 21,789 in CY24 and 44,813 in CY25 (5.5% of TIV), and year-to-date August 2026 already stands at 47,508 units (+103%) - which is 9.0% of the 530,478 YTD TIV, computed here, close to double last year's share. Charging infrastructure is the lagging leg: 6,904 public bays as at July 2026 (4,665 AC and 2,239 DC, which sum exactly) against a target of 30,000 by 2030, or 23% of the way with about three and a half years left.

The national marques are the story underneath the headline. Perodua and Proton together took 66% of 8MCY26 TIV against 54% in 8MCY25 - 41% and 25% against 38% and 16% - and both shares reconcile against the note's own monthly table. Proton is the mover: August passenger sales of 20,141 units were up 18% MoM and 38% YoY, and its year-to-date 135,166 units against 82,534 is a 63.8% increase, computed here. Perodua fell 8% on both measures. Among non-nationals in August, Toyota led with 32% share and Honda followed at 22%, with Mazda third at 5%, Chery fourth at 4% and BYD fifth at 4% - all of which reconcile against the unit table to within rounding. Order backlogs are stated marque by marque: Proton 50k units (3-6 months), Perodua 40k (2-5 months), Toyota 10k, Mazda 3.5k, Honda 3k and Nissan 1k, against an industry booking backlog of 113k units at end-August, itself down from an average 140k in 2025 on limited production capacity.

The CY26 thesis is seven-legged and two of the legs are policy delays rather than demand. Kenanga's 800k-unit forecast rests on: discounting and rebates as a share-capture strategy at the expense of margin; the new open-market-value excise duty regulation delayed to January 2027 'and potentially beyond', alongside a pre-tax CIF floor of RM200,000 for imported EVs already in force since July 2026; rising Chinese localisation through CKD tax incentives that run to 2027; sustained affordable-segment demand with national marques at an estimated 67% CY26 share; new hire-purchase rules abolishing the Rule of 78 and flat-rate loans; a stable labour market with Kenanga's own economics team forecasting 2.9% unemployment against 3% in CY25; and a value-led launch pipeline. The margin response Kenanga identifies is that manufacturers are moving away from the discounting fight - SIME into industrials, BAUTO into CBU models that the OMV rule does not touch, and HLIND into premium motorcycles. The localisation map names Chery and Jaecoo at Shah Alam, Xpeng, GWM, BAIC and SAIC at EPMB's Melaka plant, Zeekr at Proton's Tanjung Malim plant, and BYD potentially at Inokom in Kedah.

Why this row reads Positive, and the one claim a named house has since put a question mark against. The pick is declared in Kenanga's own words on page 1 - 'Our sector top picks are BAUTO... and SIME' - and repeated verbatim as a standalone heading on page 3. Searching the seven pages for this board's full conviction list returns that construction for 'top picks' and nothing for sector pick, our pick, preferred, most attractive, we like, favour or favourite, so the Kenanga Signal rests on that sentence, quoted on this row. The BYD-at-Inokom leg deserves a caveat the note does not carry: Kenanga describes Inokom as 'SIME (56%-owned with direct/indirect stakes) and BAUTO (29%-owned associate holdings)', while BIMB Securities Research, in a 15 September sector update reported by the New Straits Times, puts Sime Motors' holding at 51% and agrees on BAUTO's 29% - and adds that Inokom 'was already flagged as near full when it announced a new paint shop in 2026, so meaningful BYD volume likely requires incremental investment and lead time'. BYD's Malaysia managing director confirmed on 11 September that its own 150-acre, 50,000-unit Tanjung Malim plant had been cancelled, which is what makes a contract assembler necessary at all. Kenanga states the possibility; it does not test the capacity.

reports.name: Renewable Energy Sector Update: Another SAC Cut (CRESS Acceleration Package)
reports.catalyst: OVERWEIGHT maintained after PETRA cut the CRESS System Access Charge for firm supply to 14 sen/kWh from 20 sen/kWh on 18 September, with qualifying projects required to reach commercial operation by 31 December 2028 and to sign a minimum 10-year developer-offtaker contract. Kenanga sizes two addressable markets: about RM16bn of solar EPCC from the c.3.15GW of CRESS capacity already registered with the Single Buyer, and about RM19bn from incremental data centre demand on PETRA's projections at 30% renewable usage. It expects EPCC awards to start materialising from 4QCY26, ahead of LSS6. SLVEST is named the preferred CRESS exposure and its target price is raised to RM3.76 from RM3.36; SAMAIDEN's goes to RM2.90 from RM2.50. TENAGA's impact is called limited near term, and its target of RM16.30 matches the Company Update published in the same bundle.
reports.quote: We view the announcement positively as the 6 sen/kWh SAC reduction should foster CRESS adoption by allowing developers to offer more favourable tariff terms to offtakers, particularly DC operators.
summary: What actually changed, and how far the subsidy has moved in two years. PETRA cut the System Access Charge for firm supply to 14 sen/kWh on 18 September 2026. The note gives the full path: 25 sen/kWh when CRESS was introduced in 2024, 20 sen from 29 August 2025, and now 14 sen - a 44% reduction from the original level and 30% from the last, both computed here. Two conditions come with it: commercial operation by 31 December 2028 with no extension allowed, and a minimum 10-year developer-offtaker contract. Projects that miss the deadline revert to the prevailing SAC. On a 35 sen/kWh developer tariff and the new 14 sen SAC, Kenanga estimates equity internal rates of return of about 10-13%. It also flags what did not change: the SAC review mechanism is untouched, reviews remain once per regulatory period with variations capped at 15% during RP4, and Kenanga assumes that holds pending a revised methodology from RP5.

The two market-size numbers, both reproduced and both checked. First, 11 renewable energy developers and 8 green consumers are registered with the Single Buyer representing about 3.15GW of project capacity; at Kenanga's assumed RM5m per MW of EPCC value that is RM15.75bn, which is the c.RM16bn the note prints - arithmetic here. Second, PETRA projects Malaysian data centre power demand reaching about 21GW by 2040 against about 8.35GW of secured maximum demand today; the incremental 12.65GW at 30% renewable usage gives about 3.8GW of green energy demand, which at RM5m per MW is about RM19bn. Both chains reconcile exactly on the note's own assumptions. The timing argument that connects them to earnings is the tightest part: LSS precedent puts construction at 1.5-2 years, so an end-2028 commercial operation date forces work to start by 2H CY27, which is why Kenanga expects EPCC awards from 4QCY26 - ahead of LSS6, and therefore an order-book catalyst that arrives before the next auction cycle.

Why SLVEST rather than SAMAIDEN, and the funding arithmetic that makes the target credible. Kenanga's case rests on structure: under a 51:49 joint venture with Brookfield, SLVEST holds 51% and can participate through both EPCC and asset ownership. Its c.RM748m of unutilised funding is stated to support up to c.RM7.3bn of total project investment, which only reconciles once the JV is taken into account - RM748m as 51% of JV equity implies about RM1,466m of total equity, and at 80:20 debt-to-equity that supports RM7.33bn. The arithmetic is done here and the note does not show it. Management's target of 300-500MW of CRESS wins by year-end would need only about RM153m-255m of SLVEST equity at RM5m per MW, well inside that capacity - and those two figures reconcile exactly on the same 51% and 20% assumptions. Kenanga lifts SLVEST's FY27F/FY28F order book replenishment assumptions to RM2.1bn/RM2.0bn from RM600m/RM1.0bn, factoring in 300MW of firm-output CRESS projects, and raises its target to RM3.76 from RM3.36 on FY27F/FY28F EPS of 15.7/17.5 sen against 14.0/14.1 sen.

The two supporting names, and the one that does not reconcile. SAMAIDEN carries about RM2bn of CRESS tenders - about 70% of its utility-scale tender book, which implies a book of roughly RM2.9bn, computed here - against a comparatively low RM436m order book and a reiterated RM1bn order-book target by end-2026. Its c.RM1.4bn of unutilised funding supports up to c.RM7bn of project investment at the same 80:20 split, which reconciles exactly, and up to about 1.4GW at RM5m per MW. Its target rises to RM2.90 from RM2.50, matching the RM2.50 read from SAMAIDEN's own Results Note on this board on 27 August. KEEMING is presented as an indirect beneficiary through SLVEST's c.24% stake and its role as an M&E contractor for solar interconnection facilities, having already secured about RM126m of interconnection work from SLVEST; 300-500MW of SLVEST CRESS wins would represent RM1.5bn-2.5bn of project value, part of which could flow through. The target Kenanga states for KEEMING in the text is RM2.84 - and the note's own peer table shows RM2.00, the figure this board's 4 September row records as the previous target. See the flag.

Why this row reads Positive, and what the market and a named house did with the same announcement. The pick is declared in Kenanga's own words twice - 'We see SLVEST as our preferred CRESS exposure play' on page 1 and 'with SLVEST remaining our preferred CRESS exposure' in the conclusion. Searching the four pages for this board's full conviction list returns 'preferred' and nothing for top pick, sector pick, our pick, most attractive, we like, favour or favourite, so the Kenanga Signal rests on that word, quoted on this row. Two things sit outside the note and are worth holding beside it. The market moved on the same information before this note could be read: by mid-morning on 21 September, SOLARVEST was up 10.51% at RM3.68 - within 2.1% of Kenanga's new RM3.76 target, computed here - SAMAIDEN up 15.38% at RM2.25 and PEKAT up 5.21% at RM2.22, which is already above the RM2.10 target in Kenanga's own peer table. reports.catalyst: A deal note, not a forecast change: rating, target price and forecasts are all explicitly maintained, and both the rating and the TP carry the unchanged marker on the front page. ECOWLD won the Urban Redevelopment Authority tender for a 99-year leasehold site at Sin Ming Avenue, Bishan, Singapore, for SGD208.1m (about RM666m) - its first property development project in the city-state, earmarked for condominiums under a new VERSIONE series with a 2028 launch. Kenanga's verdict on the deal itself is NEUTRAL pending planned GDV and timeline: it calls the SGD1,612 psf ppr price 'potentially aggressive' at 11% above the second-highest of seven bids, and notes that on its own estimates ECOWLD would need to sell above SGD3,000 psf for double-digit margins while most Bishan homes transact below that mark. Set against that, it sees strategic value in retaining control and establishing a Singapore track record. OUTPERFORM and TP RM2.35 maintained.

summary: Read what this note changes before reading what it argues: nothing. The rating stays OUTPERFORM, the target price stays RM2.35, the forecast section reads 'Unchanged.' in full, and both the rating and the target carry the unchanged marker on the front page. At the RM1.96 price the target implies 19.9% upside, which matches the note's own peer table exactly. What is new is a transaction and a house view on it, and the house view is deliberately neutral: Kenanga states plainly that it will 'continue to monitor further details pertaining to the proposed development including planned GDV and development timeframe, before effecting any changes to forecast or TP'. The context the note supplies is weak share-price performance - ECOWLD down 6.2% year-to-date against a KLCI down 0.9%.

The transaction, with every stated figure reconciled. The site is approximately 46.1k sq ft with a maximum permissible gross floor area of 129.1k sq ft, taken on a 99-year lease for SGD208.1m. That gives a plot ratio of 2.80 and a land cost of SGD1,612 per square foot per plot ratio - 1,612 multiplied by 129,100 sq ft returns SGD208.1m exactly, so the psf ppr figure and the GFA are mutually consistent. Kenanga's RM666m translation implies an exchange rate of about 3.200 ringgit to the Singapore dollar; The Edge Malaysia's parallel reporting of the same deal puts it at RM667.6m, implying 3.208. At 11% above the second-highest of seven bids, the runner-up sat at roughly SGD187.5m, or about SGD1,452 psf ppr - both derived here and neither printed. The RM666m is 10.5% of ECOWLD's RM6,335.3m market capitalisation, also computed here.

The pricing test Kenanga sets, and what an independent estimate does to it. Kenanga's own threshold is explicit: on its estimates the land cost means ECOWLD 'will need to sell units at above SGD3k psf to generate double-digit margins', and it notes from source checks that most Bishan homes sell below the SGD3k mark. That is the whole basis of the 'potentially aggressive' label - a pricing requirement above the observed local market. RHB Research, publishing on the same transaction on 21 September, estimates a gross development value of RM1.3 billion for the project. Across the 129.1k sq ft of permissible GFA that is about RM10,070 per square foot, or roughly SGD3,150 at Kenanga's own implied exchange rate - just above the threshold Kenanga sets, computed here on a GFA rather than a saleable-area basis, which is a caveat since saleable area is normally smaller than GFA and would push the required rate higher still. Neither house makes that comparison.

The balance sheet and the timetable, which are where the risk actually sits. The purchase will be funded by a combination of bank financing and internal funds. Kenanga puts net gearing at 0.22x as of April 2026, rising to 0.32x assuming full bank financing - though its own Summary Earnings Table carries net gearing of 0.50x for FY26F and 0.62x for FY25A, a gap flagged on this row rather than reconciled. The timetable is long: the project is targeted for launch in 2028 under the new VERSIONE series, and Kenanga explicitly awaits 'the commencement of the project, targeted from 2028 onwards'. Nothing here touches the current or next financial year. Against that, the base business carries the forecasts: FY26F revenue of RM3,659m (+24.9%) with core net profit of RM545m (+28.8%), and FY27F of RM3,885m and RM553m (+1.4%) - so the growth is concentrated in the year now ending, and Kenanga's numbers sit within 2% of the consensus core net profit printed in the same table (RM551m and RM549m).

Why this row reads None stated, and what the note explicitly excludes. Searching the five pages for this board's full conviction list - top pick, sector pick, our pick, preferred, most attractive, we like, favour, favourite - returns nothing. Kenanga's positive language is about the transaction's strategic logic rather than the stock: it sees 'strategic value in establishing its branding and a local track record in Singapore as part of the group's efforts towards regional expansion', and argues that successful execution 'could potentially leverage its branding recognition to participate in more future tenders and partnerships opportunities'. That is a case, not a pick declaration, so the Kenanga Signal reads None stated. Three things are stated as sitting outside the RM2.35 target and must not be read into it: no planned GDV, no development timeframe and no earnings contribution from this site have been factored into forecasts at all. The named risks to the call are a slower-than-expected recovery in the local property market, changes to mortgage rates and higher construction costs.

reports.name: Tenaga Nasional Berhad
reports.catalyst: A target-price cut on a policy event, with the rating kept. After the government raised the subsidised household electricity threshold to 800kWh a month from 600kWh through end-2026, TENAGA confirmed on Friday 18 September that it will absorb the resulting RM120m-RM150m cost of exempting those consumers from the Automatic Fuel Adjustment, the RM10 monthly retail charge and SST. Kenanga views the development negatively - not for the size of the hit, which it calls manageable at under 3% of FY26 earnings, but because absorbing a cost that the IBR framework would normally pass through 'sets an uncomfortable precedent'. It books the full RM150m into 4QFY26, trims FY26 net profit 2%, and adds 25bps of equity risk premium to its cost of equity (10.69% from 10.44%), lifting WACC to 7.01% from 6.90% and cutting the DCF-derived TP to RM16.30 from RM17.00. FY27 estimates, demand growth assumptions of 5.0% and 3.5%, and the 60% payout ratio are all unchanged. OUTPERFORM maintained, with the sell-down called a buying opportunity.
reports.quote: This cost absorption sets an uncomfortable precedent and exposes TENAGA's earnings profile to elevated risk should high fuel cost persist, translating into absorption pressures into FY27.
summary: What moved and what did not. The rating stays OUTPERFORM; the target price falls 4.1% to RM16.30 from RM17.00, and it is the discount rate rather than the earnings that does most of the work. Kenanga adds 25bps of equity risk premium to its cost of equity, taking it to 10.69% from 10.44%, which lifts the WACC to 7.01% from 6.90% on an unchanged 2.0% terminal growth rate - and it says exactly why: 'to account for potential regulatory lag and execution friction in full fuel-cost pass-through under RP4'. On the earnings side only FY26 moves: the full RM150m is booked into 4QFY26, FY26 net profit is trimmed 2% to RM4,789m, FY26 NDPS is cut proportionally on an unchanged 60% payout, and FY27 is untouched at RM5,043m. Electricity demand growth assumptions of 5.0% for FY26 and 3.5% for FY27 are unchanged, and there is no ESG adjustment to the target at a 3-star rating. At RM13.04 the new target implies 25.0% upside, matching the note's own peer table.

The precedent, which is the actual subject of the note. Kenanga's concern is not the RM120m-RM150m. It is that TENAGA 'has historically been shielded by the IBR framework under the fuel-cost pass-through mechanism', and that absorbing this cost 'sets an uncomfortable precedent'. The exemption is time-boxed - it runs only through end-2026 - but the note states that 'any future policy extensions may compromise the IBR mechanism workings and introduce structural earnings volatility'. The supporting datum is that the affected consumer band is growing fast: 20% of households exceeded 600kWh in July, up from 13% in January. So the cost of each future extension rises mechanically with usage, and Kenanga offers no estimate of a FY27 extension scenario.

The size of the hit, reconciled three ways. The text gives three figures that only agree once tax is applied: a '<3% downside impact on FY26 earnings', a 2% trim to the FY26 net profit forecast, and an earnings revision of -2.3% in the Summary Earnings Table. RM150m against FY26F net profit of RM4,789m is 3.1% before tax; at the note's own 24.0% effective rate the after-tax effect is about RM114m, or 2.4% - which is the trim. That bridge is computed here and shown nowhere in the document. Two external figures make the second half of FY26 the thing to watch: The Edge Malaysia reports TENAGA's 1HFY26 net profit at RM1.99b, down 10.37%, on revenue up 7.5% to RM32.87b. Against Kenanga's full-year RM4,789m that leaves RM2.80b to be earned in 2H, a 40.7% increase half-on-half, computed here - so the forecast already embeds a sharp second-half recovery before this RM150m is deducted.

The growth case Kenanga is protecting, and the number in it that does not sit comfortably. The note's forward story is data centres: investment of more than 8,000MW by 2035, described as 30% of total Malaysian generation capacity, with about 700MW slated to come on stream this year, feeding demand growth, operating efficiency and non-regulated earnings. That 8,000MW figure is flagged on this row, because the Renewable Energy Sector Update in the same bundle puts secured data centre maximum demand at about 8.35GW today. On the balance sheet, net debt falls from RM36,797m in FY25A to RM33,705m in FY26F and RM31,030m in FY27F, taking net gearing from 0.71x to 0.63x and 0.56x, while capital expenditure stays heavy - investing cash outflows of RM14.3b and RM13.6b in FY26F and FY27F. Kenanga's FY26F net profit sits 1.4% above the consensus figure printed in its own table and FY27F 0.6% below, so the disagreement with the street is negligible, computed here.

Why this row reads None stated, and how the market and other houses took it. The note's investment case opens 'We continue to like TENAGA for: (i) its dominance in power generation, transmission and distribution in Malaysia, (ii) its defensive earnings backed by a resilient domestic economy and assets that are largely regulated, (iii) its new avenue of sustainable earnings growth fuelled by electricity demand from data centres and transmission & distribution investment..., and (iv) its heavyweight index-linked stock status.' Searching the five pages for this board's full conviction list returns only that 'We continue to like' construction and nothing for top pick, sector pick, our pick, preferred, most attractive, favour or favourite. This board treats it as investment-case language rather than a pick declaration, the same treatment given 'We like KEYFIELD' on 18 September, 'we like MISC' on 17 September and 'We like BAUTO for' on 11 September - so the Kenanga Signal reads None stated. On the market's side, The Edge Malaysia reports that TENAGA shed RM1.63b of market value on Friday 18 September, closing at RM13.04, down 2.1% from RM13.32 and its lowest close in nine months, on 23.86m shares - more than four times the previous day's volume. reports.name: Malaysia Consumer Price Index (Aug-26): Inflation edges up to 1.9% as energy costs seep back into prices
reports.catalyst: Headline inflation rose to 1.9% YoY in August from 1.8% in July, above both Kenanga's forecast and consensus of 1.8%, while core eased to 1.7% from 1.8% on a high base. reports.quote: We expect BNM to hold the OPR at 2.75% through 2026, even as the Fed and ECB resume hiking. With inflation below 2.0%, the real policy rate stays positive, giving BNM room to look through supply-driven price moves.
summary: The month was a broad monthly pickup dressed as a core deceleration. Headline CPI rose 0.3% MoM after two flat months, with 10 of 13 groups up; core also rose 0.3% MoM against 0.0% in July, led by housing and personal care costs. Yet the year-on-year core rate fell to 1.7% from 1.8%, which the note attributes explicitly to a high base. Table 2 shows the core series running 2.1%, 2.0%, 2.0%, 1.9%, 1.8%, 1.7% from March to August - six consecutive months of decline on an annual basis while the monthly rate has just turned positive. Headline over the same months reads 1.7%, 1.9%, 2.0%, 1.9%, 1.8%, 1.9%, so August is the first month since May in which headline has risen.

Where the increase came from, group by group, with the weights attached. Transport (11.3% weight) accelerated to 2.0% YoY from 1.4% as airfares surged, with domestic air travel up 15.0% MoM and diesel and petrol up 0.9% and 0.8% MoM on higher global crude. Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels (23.2% weight) rose to 2.1% from 1.8%, with electricity and gas costs climbing 3.3% against 2.0% - driven by the fuel surcharge for Peninsular households using more than 600kWh rising to 3.80 sen/kWh from 3.59 sen - alongside rentals (+0.4% MoM) and maintenance fees (+0.5% MoM). Food and beverages (29.8% weight, the largest) rose to 1.9% from 1.8% on food at home at 1.4%, with vegetables up 2.8% led by tomatoes at 38.2% and chicken up 8.0%. Personal care and miscellaneous goods and services, at 3.2%, remains the fastest-rising group in the basket.

The transmission mechanism is stated with unusual precision, and it is not the petrol pump. Kenanga writes that 'global energy prices are reaching consumers through unsubsidised channels rather than at the pump' - RON95 stays fixed at RM1.99 under BUDI95, while airfares and freight-sensitive food items continue to rise. That framing makes the electricity surcharge, rather than fuel, the visible retail channel for the oil shock, and it is the same surcharge that TENAGA agreed on 18 September to absorb: the note records that electricity bill protection now covers households using up to 800kWh, from 600kWh, from September to December, which 'caps fuel surcharge pass-through and trims headline inflation marginally in 4Q26'. So the measure that cost TENAGA RM120m-RM150m is, in Kenanga's own accounting, a small disinflationary force in the fourth quarter.

The forecast cut and the risk that cuts the other way. The 2026 inflation forecast goes to 1.9% from 2.1%, on subsidies absorbing the shock. Against that Kenanga names the key upside risk explicitly: the breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire keeps the Strait of Hormuz disrupted and crude has climbed back above USD100.0 per barrel in September - a figure this edition's own commodity table corroborates at USD100.3 for Nymex on the 18 September session. A prolonged disruption 'would raise the risk of broader second-round effects through transport, food, and production costs'. Weather-related supply disruptions are named as a further upside risk to vegetable and poultry prices into year-end, which matters given that food carries the basket's largest weight.

Malaysia is the outlier at the bottom of Kenanga's own global table, and the policy conclusion follows from it. August inflation reads 3.4% in the US, 3.2% in the EU and Indonesia, 3.1% in the UK and South Korea, 2.5% in Thailand, 1.9% in Japan and 0.8% in China. Kenanga's commentary is that the US held steady as the energy shock offset softer underlying pressure, with the Fed hiking 25bps to 3.75-4.00% 'to stop energy costs from broadening out'; that the EU matched its May peak with energy inflation at 14.3% after the Iran war and Hormuz disruption, with the ECB raising the deposit rate 25bps in September - though with core easing to 2.4% Kenanga sees 'little appetite to risk a recession over what remains a textbook supply shock'; and that China's pickup to 0.8% came from energy-driven transport prices while domestic demand stays subdued and 'export resilience continues to mask weak consumption'. The Malaysian conclusion is a hold at 2.75% through 2026, with the caveat that BNM would move only if energy costs generate persistent second-round pressures. Searching the note for this board's full conviction list returns nothing; an Economic Viewpoint carries no stock call, so the Kenanga Signal reads None stated.

reports.flag: Three points of caution on this row. (1) The opening sentence contradicts the note's own table. The text reads 'Export growth re-accelerated to 45.5% in August (Jul: 38.0%), marginally outpacing June's 45.4% growth' - but Table 1 shows June 2026 exports at 45.5% YoY, identical to August, not 45.4%. On the table's own figures August did not outpace June; it matched it. The table is the reading the rest of the document supports, since every other monthly figure in the text agrees with it. (2) One table entry is an apparent outlier. The share of intermediate goods in total imports is printed as 30.7 for April 2026, against a range of 46.8 to 55.6 in every other month shown and 47.1 in March. No text discusses April's share and the figure cannot be verified from the retrieved source; reported as printed and not used. (3) Two figures in the text come from outside the table and cannot be cross-checked against it. The year-to-date export growth of 31.2% (Jan-Jul: 29.2%) and the claim that exports are 'on track to exceed RM2.0 trillion mark this year' have no supporting level anywhere in the note - Table 1 carries growth rates and the trade balance in ringgit, but no export value. Both were corroborated instead against an independent named source: MATRADE, reported by the New Straits Times on 21 September, puts Jan-Aug 2026 exports at RM1.356 trillion, up 31.2% from RM1.033 trillion. This is an Economic Viewpoint and carries no stock call, so the rating, target-price and share-price columns are empty by design and no Analyst Signal is sought.
reports.name: Malaysia External Trade (Aug-26): Exports surge on strong chip demand; trade bet holds despite seasonal pullback
reports.catalyst: Export growth re-accelerated to 45.5% YoY in August from 38.0% in July, beating consensus of 38.0% and Kenanga's own estimate of 44.4%; imports rose 41.1% against a 33.3% consensus but slightly below Kenanga's 41.8%. The trade surplus widened to RM28.1b from RM22.5b, ahead of both consensus (RM25.3b) and Kenanga's estimate (RM25.9b). Electrical and electronic exports surged to a four-month high of 66.5% and shipments to the United States jumped to a record 139.1%. On the strength of it Kenanga raises its 2026 export forecast to 28.5% from 19.0%, with exports on track to exceed RM2.0 trillion this year, and maintains its 2026 GDP growth forecast at 5.3% (2025: 5.2%) - while cautioning that both exports and imports fell month-on-month and that growth should slow in 2H26 as base effects fade.
reports.quote: We've raised our 2026 export forecast to 28.5% (2025: 6.6%) from 19.0%, with exports value on track to exceed RM2.0 trillion mark this year.
summary: The headline is a beat on every line and the surplus is the cleanest read. Exports +45.5% against a 38.0% consensus and a 44.4% house estimate; imports +41.1% against 33.3% consensus and 41.8% house; total trade +43.4%; and a surplus of RM28.1b against RM25.3b consensus and RM25.9b house, up from RM22.5b in July. Those figures reconcile exactly against the same day's digest, which prints MITI's exports of RM191.05b, imports of RM162.96b and total trade of RM354.01b - the difference is RM28.09b and the sum is RM354.01b, both computed here. The +45.5% growth also implies an August 2025 base of about RM131.3b, derived here and printed nowhere.

It is a chip story with a single dominant destination, and that is the concentration risk. By sector, manufacturing strengthened to 50.4% from 42.6% and mining accelerated to 43.3% from 9.6%, offsetting a 21.4% collapse in agriculture from +4.8%. By product, electrical and electronic exports hit a four-month high of 66.5% from 51.0% while their share of total exports narrowed slightly to 48.4% from 49.4% - so close to half the export book is E&E. By destination, shipments to the United States jumped to a record 139.1% from 81.5%, with Singapore at 61.5%, Taiwan 105.2%, Hong Kong 79.7%, Japan 55.6% and South Korea 9.4%, while China moderated to 22.9% from 31.2% and the EU to 20.0% from 37.0%. The item this board carries as its lead global macro bit in the same edition is the Trump-Xi trade meeting; nothing in this note addresses what a tariff outcome would do to a record US channel.

The import side says the production cycle is real rather than a re-export artefact. Both re-exports (43.3%) and retained imports (40.4%) expanded. By end use, intermediate goods hit a four-year high of 50.5% from 40.8%, which Kenanga reads as robust production momentum, and capital goods jumped 37.4% from 23.8%, which it reads as continued investment activity. Consumption goods went the other way at -1.6% from +5.2% - the only negative end-use category and, notably, the one that tracks domestic demand rather than the export machine. By product, imports were driven by E&E at 89.3% from 58.3% and a rebound in crude petroleum at 87.0% from -44.4%.

Underneath the record, the month actually shrank. Exports fell 1.3% MoM after an 8.8% July rebound and imports 4.7% after 5.5%, with total trade down 2.9%. Kenanga calls both 'a typical seasonal correction' and 'consistent with the seasonal pullback', which the table supports - the MoM series has alternated sign repeatedly through 2026. The forward guidance is correspondingly two-handed: year-to-date growth expanded to 31.2% from 29.2% for January-July, sustained by AI-driven technology investment and new product launches, but Kenanga expects export growth to slow in 2H26 as favourable base effects fade. The named downside risks are renewed US trade-policy uncertainty, weaker global growth amid higher energy prices and restrictive monetary conditions, geopolitical tension, 'a possible electronics demand cliff post AI-driven investment cycle', and commodity volatility.

The RM2.0 trillion claim can be checked against an independent named source, and it holds. MATRADE, reported by the New Straits Times on 21 September, puts January-August 2026 exports at RM1.356 trillion against RM1.033 trillion a year earlier - the same 31.2% Kenanga carries, now with a level attached. RM1.356 trillion over eight months annualises to about RM2.03 trillion at a flat run-rate, computed here, so the forecast requires no acceleration at all, only that the pace holds. MATRADE adds that exports to 40 countries, including the United States, France and Ireland, have already surpassed their full-year 2025 values, with emerging-market growth led by Namibia (+430.6%), Angola (+215.4%), Ethiopia (+51.2%), Tanzania (+50.2%) and Bangladesh (+20.2%). Kenanga's GDP conclusion is a maintained 5.3% for 2026, the same standing figure this board has carried since 1 September, with the note adding that continued momentum 'could push 2H26 results, and full-year GDP, above forecast'. Searching the note for this board's full conviction list returns nothing; an Economic Viewpoint carries no stock call, so the Kenanga Signal reads None stated.

reports.flag: Three points of caution on this row. (1) Three different Japanese inflation figures appear across this bundle without being reconciled. This note states that 'core CPI has risen moderately to a 1.5-2.0% range' and that 'August core CPI eased'; its own Table 2 shows the Bank of Japan's July forecast for fiscal 2026 core CPI at +2.3% to +2.7% with a +2.5% median; and Kenanga's CPI Economic Viewpoint published in the same bundle prints Japan's headline inflation flat at 1.9% for both July and August. The three are different series - underlying inflation, BoJ core excluding fresh food, and headline - but no source says so, and the note gives no level or month for the August core figure it describes as easing. Reported as printed rather than resolved. (2) The neutral-rate claim is unsupported by any figure. The note states that at 1.25% 'the policy rate sits inside the lower end of the BoJ's estimated neutral range for the first time' without printing that range anywhere, so the claim cannot be checked from the retrieved source. Table 3 shows the KIBB outlook for the 15-16 June meeting as 'No change' against an actual 25bps hike, and for the 17-18 September meeting as '25 bps hike' against an actual 25bps hike.
