reports.name: BoJ Monetary Policy Decision (17-18 September): 1.25% done, two dissents push the next hike to 1Q27
reports.catalyst: The Bank of Japan raised the overnight call rate 25bps to 1.25% in a 7-2 vote, three months after June's hike, and Kenanga says the rate now sits inside the lower end of the BoJ's estimated neutral range for the first time. Board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissented, both on dovish grounds. The BoJ kept its tightening bias and flagged a new priority - stabilising underlying inflation at around 2.0% to stop it overshooting - while the board voted unanimously to switch the climate response financing operation to a floating loan rate tied to the complementary deposit facility rate, capped at JPY50.0t in total and JPY10.0t per counterparty. Kenanga pushes its next 25bps hike call to 1Q27 on the divided board, Governor Ueda declining to set a pace, and easing August core CPI, and maintains its end-2026 USDJPY forecast at 154.0 while conceding near-term risk towards 158-160.
reports.quote: We maintain our end-2026 USDJPY forecast at 154.0 on the view that this repricing proves temporary: an extended Fed hold, continued BoJ normalisation and the standing threat of further intervention should gradually narrow the US-Japan rate gap and pull the pair back over the fourth quarter.
summary: The vote is the whole argument. A 25bps hike to 1.25% passed 7-2, and both dissents are dovish: Toichiro Asada argued the economy was not strong enough to justify a hike with core CPI running below 2.0% recently, and Ayano Sato judged that economic and price developments had not accelerated materially. That is why Kenanga reads a tightening decision as a signal to slow down rather than speed up - 'this decision does not lock the BoJ into a quarterly cadence', Ueda declined to set a pace, 'the dissents raise the bar for another move this year', and August core CPI eased. The next 25bps hike is pushed to 1Q27, with faster inflation, yen weakness or high energy costs named as the things that could bring it forward. Kenanga's own meeting table is consistent with that: 'No change' is its call for both remaining 2026 meetings, on 29-30 October and 17-18 December.

The BoJ has changed what it is worried about, and the note says so plainly. Alongside the tightening bias the central bank 'flagged a new priority: stabilising underlying CPI inflation at around 2.0%, to stop inflation from overshooting and hurting the economy later'. On the inflation outlook it now flags an upside risk that underlying inflation overshoots 2.0% as firms lean harder into raising wages and prices and longer-term expectations climb - and expects underlying inflation to reach a level broadly consistent with the 2.0% target between 2H26 and 2027. Ueda 'signalled pre-emptive action' and 'did not rule out larger or consecutive hikes, but tied them to a clear overshoot Japan has yet to see'. That is a conditional hawk: the trigger is named and has not fired.

The economic backdrop is described as moderate with a supply-shock caveat. Japan's economy 'has recovered moderately, with some pockets of weakness, partly because of the West Asia conflict', and growth is expected to continue at a moderate but slower pace. Oil prices elevated since early spring weigh on activity; government measures, accommodative financial conditions and global AI-related demand provide support. Exports and industrial production have started to pick up, corporate profits remain high, private consumption holds up despite weak household sentiment, and housing investment continues to decline. The BoJ's own July forecasts, reproduced in the note, have real GDP at +0.6% for fiscal 2026 and +0.8% for both fiscal 2027 and 2028, with core CPI medians of +2.5%, +2.4% and +2.0% - so the BoJ expects its own core measure above target for two more years.

The currency call is the part with the sharpest near-term test, and spot has already moved against it. Ueda stressed that the BoJ does not set policy to steer or cap the yen and watches FX only for its effect on domestic inflation. Kenanga sees this in two stages: near term, markets pricing a second Fed hike and elevated oil could push USDJPY to 158-160; thereafter an extended Fed hold, continued BoJ normalisation and the standing threat of intervention should pull it back. It maintains end-2026 at 154.0 and names the trigger explicitly - 'the Fed holding rather than delivering a second hike; without it, 154.0 is at risk to the upside'. This edition's own forex table prints USD/YEN at 156.88 on the 18 September session, up 0.79%, which is already 1.9% above the year-end forecast and inside the lower half of the stated near-term range, computed here. Kenanga's Bond Market Weekly Outlook in the same bundle takes the same view from the rates side, with a base case that the latest Fed hike marks the end of the tightening cycle.

The operational decision is small but worth recording because it was unanimous where the rate was not. The board voted unanimously to switch the climate response financing operation to a floating loan rate tied to the complementary deposit facility rate, capping total loans at JPY50.0t and loans per counterparty at JPY10.0t, and extended the same floating-rate approach to the disaster area and pooled collateral operations. On the international comparison, Kenanga's own table of thirteen policy rates puts Japan's 1.25% second-lowest, above only Thailand at 1.00%, against the US at 3.75-4.00%, the euro area at 2.50%, New Zealand at 2.75%, the Philippines at 5.00%, South Korea at 3.00%, Indonesia at 5.75% and Australia at 4.35% - with Malaysia at 2.75% and its last move a 25bps cut in July 2025. Searching the note for this board's full conviction list returns nothing; an Economic Viewpoint carries no stock call, so the Kenanga Signal reads None stated.

reports.flag: Four points of caution on this row, reported as printed rather than resolved. (1) The note's Bursa equity flow figure is contradicted by this board's own daily record, which reconciles exactly to two named non-Kenanga houses. The note states that 'foreign institutions also remained net sellers of Bursa Malaysia, posting RM160.3m of net outflows from Bursa Malaysia'. The four trading sessions of the week ended 18 September - 14, 15, 17 and 18 September, with 16 September a public holiday - are recorded on this board, from Kenanga's own digests, as foreign net flows of +RM50.6m, -RM17.5m, +RM37.3m and +RM56.5m, a net inflow of RM126.9m, computed here. BIMB Securities Research, reported by the New Straits Times on 21 September, puts the same week at a net inflow of RM127m, and MBSB Research separately identifies foreign institutions as net buyers on three of the four days with the largest inflow on Friday at RM56.5m, followed by Monday at RM50.6m and Thursday at RM37.3m - all three matching this board's figures exactly. The same reconciliation holds for the other two participant groups: local institutions sum to -RM368.0m against BIMB's RM368m net outflow, and retail to +RM241.2m against BIMB's RM241m. The RM160.3m outflow figure is therefore recorded here as printed and is not used as data. Note that the note's separate bond-flow figure - foreign investors pulling RM2.0b from Malaysian bonds - is a different market and is not contradicted by anything retrieved. (2) The week's price column is labelled 'Yesterday' in Table 3 while carrying the date 18/09/26; this report is dated Monday 21 September, so the column describes last Friday. (3) The Q3-26 forecasts in Table 1 are already overtaken by spot with days of the quarter left: 10-year MGS is forecast at 3.95% against an actual 3.917% on 18 September, and USDMYR at 4.05 against 4.0817 in this edition's own forex table. Both comparisons are arithmetic here. (4) Typographical slips carried as printed: the outlook paragraph reads 'We expect policy rates expected to remain unchanged through end-2027', and the page headers on pages 2 and 3 read '6 S' and 'ENANGA INVESTMENT BANK BERHAD'. This is an Economic Viewpoint and carries no stock call, so the rating, target-price and share-price columns are empty by design and no Analyst Signal is sought.
reports.name: Bond Market Weekly Outlook: Local yields hold steady post-FOMC; geopolitical risks emerge as key driver
reports.catalyst: MGS and GII yields fell sharply across the curve in the week to 18 September, declining between 4.5bps and 28.9bps, with the 10-year MGS down 26.7bps to 3.917% and the 10-year GII down 21.4bps to 3.939%. Kenanga attributes the rally to the FOMC's anticipated 25bps hike removing event risk and fuelling duration demand, Brent easing as Saudi Arabia restored part of its East-West pipeline capacity, August exports surging 45.5%, a bilateral swap arrangement with Japan, and the government's electricity relief threshold decision. US Treasuries went the other way, with the 10-year up 2.9bps to 4.996% and the 2-year up 11.8bps to 4.743%. Kenanga expects local yields to stay rangebound absent domestic catalysts, with focus on the US-Iran conflict and the Trump-Xi meeting, and holds a base case that the latest Fed hike ends the tightening cycle with policy rates unchanged through end-2027.
reports.quote: MGS yields reversed sharply lower after the FOMC's anticipated 25 bps hike removed event risk and fuelled duration demand.
summary: The size of the move, with the stated range checked against the table. MGS and GII yields are described as falling 'between 4.5 bps to 28.9 bps' and Table 3 bears that out exactly at both ends - the 3-year GII fell 4.5bps and the 15-year MGS 28.9bps. The belly and long end did the work: 20-year MGS -27.3bps, 10-year MGS -26.7bps to 3.917%, 7-year -24.0bps, against just -8.3bps at 5 years and -12.9bps at 3 years. That is a bull flattening of the long end, and it directly reverses the steepening that Kenanga attributed to a rebuilt term premium ahead of Budget 2027 in its 17 September Economic Viewpoint, carried on this board. Even after the rally the year-to-date picture remains a bear market: 10-year MGS is up 42.5bps in 2026 and up 51.4bps year-on-year, and every MGS and GII tenor in the table is higher than it was on 1 January.

US Treasuries moved the opposite way and the differential is now deeply negative. UST yields were mixed between -2.7bps and +11.8bps, with the front end selling off - 2-year +11.8bps to 4.743%, 3-year +11.6bps, 5-year +7.4bps - while the 30-year fell 2.7bps. The 10-year rose 2.9bps to 4.996%. Against the 10-year MGS at 3.917% that leaves the Malaysia-US 10-year differential at about -107.9bps, computed here. Kenanga's explanation for the divergence is positioning rather than fundamentals: 'the Fed and BoJ delivered widely anticipated rate hikes into lighter pre-hike positioning', with strong August retail sales and a surprise decline in initial jobless claims suggesting an extended Fed hold. Its base case is explicit - 'the latest Fed hike marks the end of the tightening cycle', with policy rates unchanged through end-2027.

The forecast table is the most forward-looking thing in the bundle, and spot has already passed part of it. Table 1 gives 10-year MGS at 3.95% for Q3-26, 3.88% for Q4-26, 3.87% for Q1-27 and 3.78% for Q2-27; UST at 4.85%, 4.80%, 4.75% and 4.69%; USDMYR at 4.05, 3.95, 4.00 and 4.02; and the OPR flat at 2.75% throughout. The Q4-26 figures for MGS, USDMYR and the OPR are identical to the standing end-2026 forecasts this board carried from 17 September, so nothing has been revised. But with under two weeks of the quarter left, the 10-year MGS at 3.917% has already fallen below the 3.95% Q3 forecast, and USDMYR at 4.0817 in this edition's forex table sits above the 4.05 Q3 forecast - both computed here. Note also the ringgit path: Kenanga has it strengthening to 3.95 by end-2026 and then weakening again to 4.00 and 4.02 through 1H27.

A risk this board flagged three days ago has got sharper, and this note supplies the number. On 18 September this board carried a report that Malaysia's bonds face a growing risk of Japanese fund outflows because the 10-year Malaysia-Japan yield premium had compressed to around 112bps against a five-year average of 278bps. Table 3 here lets that be updated: 10-year MGS at 3.917% against the 10-year Japanese government bond at 2.989% is a premium of 92.8bps as at 18 September, down from 119.7bps a week earlier - computed here from the note's own figures. The MGS rally has therefore narrowed the premium by a further 27bps in one week, to roughly a third of the five-year average. Neither source connects them. On the flow side Kenanga records foreign investors turning net sellers of RM2.0b of Malaysian bonds last week, which cuts against the argument in its own 17 September Market Strategy that foreigners remained net buyers - though the equity flow figure in the same paragraph does not survive checking, and is flagged on this row.

What the note says is driving the market next is not domestic. Kenanga expects local yields 'to remain largely rangebound in the near term amid the absence of major domestic catalysts', with investor focus instead on the evolving US-Iran conflict and the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting - the latter being this edition's lead global macro item, which the digest itself carries with no date, agenda or participants beyond the two principals. Kenanga states the direction of the trade explicitly: 'any trade or de-escalation breakthrough would likely reduce UST duration demand', meaning a good outcome is a yield-negative one for bonds. On supply, there was no reopening or issuance in the week; the next auction is a reopening of the 7-year MGS with RM5.0b to be issued and no private placement. The 2026 issuance programme to date stands at RM50.0b of MGS reopenings and RM15.0b of new MGS, with the same split for GII, against RM67.5b/RM15.0b and RM61.5b/RM24.5b in 2025. Searching the note for this board's full conviction list returns nothing; an Economic Viewpoint carries no stock call, so the Kenanga Signal reads None stated.
